title: Electrical short circuit
summary: An overloaded extension board sparks, your cousin grabs the cable, and a curtain starts to burn. Cut the power and stay safe.
sources: National Disaster Management Authority (India): fire safety guidance
Bureau of Indian Standards / electricity board consumer safety advice: isolate at the MCB or main switch
St John Ambulance / Indian Red Cross Society first aid: electric shock

scenes.narration: You're charging a laptop from an extension board crowded with plugs. There's a burning-plastic smell, a crackle, and sparks jump from the board.
scenes.prompt: Spot the danger. Pick "Point it out" and tap where it is.

hints.text: A burning smell, a crackle and sparks: where is it coming from? And should anyone touch it?
Look at the crowded extension board.
Pick "Point it out" and use it on the extension board, then keep away from it.

choices.label: Point at the board: that's an electrical fault, keep away from it
choices.feedback: Right. Sparks, crackling and a burning smell mean an electrical fault that can start a fire. Keep your hands off it.

choices.label: It's just the laptop charger getting warm. Ignore it.
choices.feedback: Sparks and burning smells are never normal. Overloaded boards cause many house fires.

choices.label: Wiggle the plugs to stop the crackling
choices.feedback: Don't touch a sparking board: you could get a shock or a burn. Cut the power at the MCB instead.

scenes.narration: Your cousin grabs the charger cable to yank it out. The insulation has melted and she freezes, unable to let go: she's being shocked. The MCB box is on the wall by the door.
scenes.prompt: Help her without becoming a second casualty.

hints.text: If you touch someone who is being shocked, the current can flow through you too. What stops the current at its source?
Look at the wall by the door: the MCB box.
Use your hands on the MCB box: switch the main power off. Don't touch your cousin until it's off.

choices.label: Switch off the power at the MCB / main switch
choices.feedback: Yes. Cutting the supply at the MCB or main switch stops the current, and then she can be helped safely.

choices.label: Stand on something dry and push the cable away with a dry wooden broom handle
choices.feedback: That's what to do if you can't reach the power switch. Here the MCB was close, and switching it off is safer and quicker.

choices.label: Grab her arm and pull her away
choices.feedback: Never touch someone who is being shocked: the current can pass into you too. Cut the power first, or use a dry wooden object. (Your uncle runs in and switches off the MCB.)

choices.label: Throw water on the sparking board
choices.feedback: Water conducts electricity: it can spread the shock to you and everyone standing in it. (Your uncle runs in and switches off the MCB.)

scenes.narration: The power is off and your cousin has let go. But the melted board has set the bottom of the curtain alight: small flames, for now. There's a CO₂ and a dry powder extinguisher by the door.

hints.text: The power is off, but there's a fire. Water and electrics don't mix. Which extinguisher is safe here, or is getting out the right call?
Look at the burning curtain, and keep the door behind you.
Aim the CO₂ extinguisher at the base of the curtain fire. If it grows, get out, close the door and call 112.

choices.label: Aim the CO₂ extinguisher at the base of the small fire, with the door behind you
choices.feedback: Right. CO₂ (or dry powder) is safe on electrical fires. Aim at the base and sweep. Only tackle a small fire with a clear way out behind you.

choices.label: Use the dry powder extinguisher on the base of the fire
choices.feedback: Yes. A dry powder (ABC) extinguisher works on electrical and fabric fires. Aim at the base, sweep side to side, and keep your exit behind you.

choices.label: Get everyone out, close the door, and call 112
choices.feedback: Always a safe choice. Once a fire spreads to furnishings, getting out and closing the door is right. Firefighters put it out.

choices.label: Throw the bucket of water at the curtain and board
choices.feedback: Even with the MCB off, an inverter, UPS or wrong circuit can keep things live. Water conducts. Use CO₂ or dry powder, never water, near electrics.

choices.label: Beat the curtain flames with a towel
choices.feedback: Beating flames fans them and sends burning bits flying. Use an extinguisher on a small fire, or get out and close the door.

scenes.narration: The fire is out and the smoke is clearing. Your cousin says she feels fine, but there's a small mark on her palm where she held the cable.

hints.text: An electric shock can hurt the inside of the body even when the person feels fine. Who should check her?
Look at your cousin and the mark on her palm.
Use the phone on your cousin: call 112 or get her checked by a doctor today.

choices.label: Call 112 / get her checked by a doctor, even though she feels fine
choices.feedback: Right. Anyone who has had an electric shock needs a medical check: it can affect the heartbeat, and burns can be deeper than they look.

choices.label: She says she's fine, so carry on
choices.feedback: After an electric shock, always get a medical check, even if the person feels fine.

choices.label: Switch the MCB back on to see if the board still works
choices.feedback: Never restore power to a burnt circuit. Unplug the damaged board and get an electrician to check the wiring first.

end-safe.text: The doctor checks your cousin's heart and dresses the small burn. An electrician finds the board was badly overloaded and replaces it.

end-unsafe.text: Switching the power back on made the burnt board arc again and the room filled with smoke. Never restore power until an electrician has checked it.

learn: Sparks, crackles and burning smells mean an electrical fault: don't touch it.
Switch off at the MCB or main switch first. Never touch someone being shocked.
If you can't reach the switch, stand on something dry and push them clear with a dry wooden object.
Never use water on or near electrics. Use a CO₂ or dry powder extinguisher on a small fire, or get out and call 112.
Anyone who has had an electric shock needs a medical check. Don't overload extension boards.
disclaimer: Training only. This is not a substitute for emergency services or certified first-aid and fire-safety training. In a real emergency in India, call 112.
